newsitem.title: RUSSIA: YELTSIN PICKS TOP REGIONAL REFORMER FOR CABINET.
newsitem.headline: YELTSIN PICKS TOP REGIONAL REFORMER FOR CABINET.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin offered a top cabinet job on Monday to an influential and liberal regional leader, Boris Nemtsov, sending another signal of his commitment to boosting Russia's stalled economic reforms.

Yeltsin offered Nemtsov, the 37-year-old dynamic governor of the Nizhny Novgorod region, the chance to be one of two first deputy prime ministers with close aide Anatoly Chubais as part of a cabinet reshuffle which is being slowly unveiled.
The Kremlin later said Nemtsov had accepted.
"There is a very interesting variant," Yeltsin, confident, smiling and energetic, was shown on television as telling a slightly concerned-looking Nemtsov.

"Two young men -- you and Anatoly Chubais -- create a fresh young team in the government -- from scratch. No one (else) has been appointed yet. All candidates to the government would be agreed with the two first deputy premiers."

Interfax said Nemtsov, seen as a potential presidential candidate in the year 2000, had accepted the offer and would handle the government's social programmes, natural monopolies and deal with powerful regional authorities.
Yeltsin was due to meet Chubais and Chernomyrdin later on Monday to discuss the government reshuffle.

Yeltsin, worried by the growing tension caused by chronic delaysin wages and the government's inability to handle the crisis, has told Chernomyrdin to review the structure of the cabinet and dramatically improve its performance.

He has sent Chubais, his 41-year-old chief of staff with a reputation as a tough organiser, to reinforce the government and had promised that he would be the only first deputy premier. But the rest of the cabinet line-up has been slow to emerge.

Political analysts have suggested that the stalemate has been partly caused by horse-trading between powerful political rivals, Chubais and Chernomyrdin, over who is in the government and which of them plays first fiddle.
Initial leaks from the Kremlin signalled that the number of deputy prime ministers in the new cabinet would be only four but Yeltsin later said there would be seven.
"There is the premier and the first deputy premier, who is in charge of the economy and who controls the country's finance," Interfax quoted governor of Samara region, Konstantin Titov, as saying.
"In this situation, the opinion of one of them is not always similar to the opinion of another," he added. "It is problematic if (they) work in such conditions."
It was not clear how the appointment of Nemtsov, who could be a rival to Chernomyrdin in the next presidential election in the year 2000, will change the balance of power in the Kremlin.
But Yeltsin is expected to announce his decisions on the government before he heads to Helsinki for a summit with President Bill Clinton on Thursday and Friday.
U.S. and Russian officials have been trying to hammer out a deal that Yeltsin and Clinton can announce to ease tensions over NATO's expansion plans.

Yeltsin has laid out stiff terms for any softening of Moscow's objections to NATO's plans, saying he would insist on a legally-binding treaty barring Western forces from being stationed in eastern Europe.

Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov held talks in Washington over the weekend to try to forge a breakthrough before the summit, but U.S. officials remain publically opposed to a legally binding treaty and other Russian demands.
The start of the two-day summit has been postponed for a day, until Thursday, to allow Clinton to recover from knee surgery after a fall last week.
